content: Roseola is a disease that primarily affects infants. It is characterized by a sudden and significant increase in body temperature, which can reach as high as 40°C (104°F). This febrile phase is followed by a rapid return to normal body temperature within 2 to 4 days, coinciding with the appearance of a maculopapular rash. The rash is erythematous and typically lasts for 1 to 3 days. Roseola is generally a benign condition that resolves without any long-term complications. The disease is caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), which has two distinct species: HHV-6A and HHV-6B. The first description of roseola as a febrile exanthem in infants was provided by Zahorsky in 1910. Human Herpesvirus 6 was later identified in 1986. There is no established classification system for roseola. The pathophysiology of roseola involves two distinct phases: the febrile phase and the rash phase. During the febrile phase, HHV-6 replicates in the salivary glands and is secreted, serving as the primary source of infection. After the fever resolves, the virus enters a latent phase within lymphocytes and monocytes, leading to the onset of the rash phase. In older children, immunocompromised adults, and organ transplant recipients, a more severe form of HHV-6 infection can occur. Roseola is caused by Human Herpesvirus 6, a member of the Herpesvirales order, Herpesviridae family, Betaherpesvirinae subfamily, and Roseolovirus genus. Herpesviruses have a unique four-layered structure. The core contains a large, double-stranded DNA genome, which is enclosed by an icosapentahedral capsid composed of capsomers. Surrounding the capsid is an amorphous protein coat called the tegument, which is further encased in a glycoprotein-bearing lipid bilayer envelope. Roseola must be differentiated from other febrile illnesses that present with a rash, such as rubella (German measles), rubeola (measles), hand-foot-and-mouth disease caused by coxsackievirus, erythema infectiosum caused by parvovirus B19, scarlet fever, and even drug allergies. There is no accurate data on the prevalence or incidence of roseola, as it is a self-limiting disease and often underreported. Roseola primarily affects young children, with peak prevalence occurring between 7 and 13 months of age. Ninety percent of cases occur in children under the age of two. The disease affects boys and girls equally and can occur throughout the year, although outbreaks may be seasonal. Common risk factors for developing roseola include infancy (under two years of age), immunosuppression, and organ transplantation. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) states that there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for roseola. The symptoms of roseola typically begin within the first two years of life. If left untreated, the disease resolves on its own. Rare complications include febrile seizures, encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, thrombocytopenic purpura, bone marrow failure, and pneumonitis. However, the overall prognosis for roseola is excellent. The hallmark symptom of roseola is a non-itchy macular or maculopapular rash. A history of high fever, reaching 40°C (104°F) and lasting for 3 to 5 days, is also characteristic. Physical examination findings depend on the phase of the disease. During the febrile phase, vital signs are affected, while in the rash phase, vital signs normalize, and skin changes become apparent. The diagnosis of roseola is primarily clinical. In atypical cases, serologic testing and direct detection of HHV-6 in saliva can confirm the diagnosis. Diagnostic methods include antigen detection, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and immunofluorescence. There are no findings associated with roseola on electrocardiograms, chest X-rays, MRIs, echocardiography, or other imaging studies. There is no specific treatment for roseola, as it is a self-limiting disease that resolves without medical intervention. Supportive therapy, such as antipyretics, can be used to manage high fever. Surgical intervention is not recommended for roseola. There is no established method for preventing roseola. However, standard sanitary practices, such as handwashing, can help reduce the spread of HHV-6. There are no secondary preventive measures available for roseola.
